sections.heading: OCR Evaluation and Post-Correction
sections.evidence: Optical character recognition (OCR) converts document images into machine-readable text, but evaluating an OCR system is not simply a matter of asking how many characters it recognized correctly. The observed error rate depends on what is treated as ground truth, how text is normalized, what counts as a character or word, how reading order and segmentation are represented, which alignment algorithm is used, and whether the system is evaluated before or after post-correction.
paragraphs: Optical character recognition (OCR) converts document images into machine-readable text, but evaluating an OCR system is not simply a matter of asking how many characters it recognized correctly. The observed error rate depends on what is treated as ground truth, how text is normalized, what counts as a character or word, how reading order and segmentation are represented, which alignment algorithm is used, and whether the system is evaluated before or after post-correction.

Post-correction adds another layer of difficulty. A correction system can remove genuine OCR errors, leave errors untouched, or damage text that was already correct. A method that aggressively rewrites noisy text may reduce one aggregate edit-distance metric while destroying historically meaningful spellings, proper names, numerical values, punctuation, or document-specific terminology.
OCR quality should therefore be modeled as a pipeline:
document image | v layout / region analysis | v line and word segmentation | v character / sequence recognition | v raw OCR text | v post-correction | v final machine-readable text | v downstream use
Different evaluation questions belong at different points in this pipeline.

Character error rate may be appropriate for measuring transcription fidelity. Word error rate may better expose the effect of character errors on lexical usability. Layout metrics are required when reading order matters. Post-correction additionally requires measures of how many real errors were repaired and how many new errors were introduced.
OCR evaluation != one universal accuracy number.

sections.heading: 1. What exactly is being evaluated?
sections.evidence: Before selecting a metric, define the target object.
paragraphs: Before selecting a metric, define the target object.

Evaluation target Question Typical evidence Layout detection Were regions, columns, tables, marginalia, and other structures identified correctly? Regions, polygons, classes, reading order Text-line segmentation Were text lines separated correctly? Line boundaries and baselines Character recognition Was the visual text transcribed faithfully? Character or grapheme sequence Word recognition How many lexical units were recovered correctly? Token sequences Reading order Is text serialized in the intended document order? Ordered regions and lines Post-correction Did correction reduce OCR noise without damaging valid text? Raw OCR, corrected OCR, ground truth Downstream utility Can the text support search, NLP, extraction, or scholarly use? Task-specific performance
A system can perform well at one level and badly at another.
For example, a two-column page may contain nearly perfect character recognition but an incorrect reading order:
GROUND TRUTH: Column A line 1 Column A line 2 Column A line 3 Column B line 1 Column B line 2 Column B line 3
A layout system might instead serialize:
Column A line 1 Column B line 1 Column A line 2 Column B line 2 Column A line 3 Column B line 3
Almost every character can be recognized correctly while the serialized document becomes severely corrupted.
This distinction is central to serious OCR benchmarking.

sections.heading: 2. Ground truth is part of the measurement system
sections.evidence: OCR evaluation requires a reference transcription, commonly called ground truth (GT).
paragraphs: OCR evaluation requires a reference transcription, commonly called ground truth (GT).
image | +----> human / curated reference transcription = GT | +----> OCR system output = hypothesis
The two textual representations are then compared.
But ground truth is not an abstract property of the page. It is an annotation created according to a transcription policy.
The reference must answer questions such as:
Should long s ( ſ ) remain distinct from modern s ?
Should ligatures be retained or decomposed?
Should damaged or unreadable characters receive special symbols?
Should capitalization be diplomatic or normalized?
Should page headers and footers be included?
Which Unicode normalization form should be used?

The OCR-D project explicitly treats OCR evaluation as comparison against representative ground truth and provides detailed ground-truth conventions for historical document processing. See the OCR-D Ground Truth Guidelines .
visual source + transcription policy + encoding policy + segmentation policy + reading-order policy.

sections.heading: 4. The mathematical core: edit distance
sections.evidence: Most text-level OCR evaluation begins with an alignment between a reference sequence and an OCR sequence.
paragraphs: Most text-level OCR evaluation begins with an alignment between a reference sequence and an OCR sequence.
The standard sequence comparison uses insertion, deletion, and substitution operations:
substitution: one reference symbol is recognized as another;
deletion: a reference symbol is missing;
insertion: OCR introduces an additional symbol.
With unit costs, the minimum number of such operations is the Levenshtein distance .
cost = 0 if ri = hj 1 otherwise d[i][j] = min( d[i-1][j] + 1, # deletion d[i][j-1] + 1, # insertion d[i-1][j-1] + cost # match / substitution )
The full algorithmic structure is discussed in the Wagner-Fischer algorithm .

sections.heading: 8. What counts as a character?
sections.evidence: This question becomes surprisingly important in Unicode text.
paragraphs: This question becomes surprisingly important in Unicode text.
A visual character may correspond to:
a historical or Private Use Area encoding.
For example, an accented character may be represented as:
U+0065 U+0301 e + combining acute accent
These may appear identical to a reader but contain different numbers of Unicode code points.
The Unicode Standard explicitly distinguishes code points from grapheme clusters. See Unicode Standard Annex #29: Unicode Text Segmentation .
OCR-D defines a character for its text-evaluation framework as a grapheme cluster and uses NFC-normalized representations.
This is a defensible choice, but it demonstrates that:
CER cannot be reproduced without defining the evaluation unit.
The implementation consequences are examined more generally in Unicode- and grapheme-safe Levenshtein computation .

sections.heading: 9. Unicode normalization and OCR evaluation
sections.evidence: Before edit-distance evaluation, reference and hypothesis should normally follow a documented Unicode policy.
paragraphs: Before edit-distance evaluation, reference and hypothesis should normally follow a documented Unicode policy.
But normalization is not a cosmetic implementation detail.
Canonical normalization may legitimately remove representational differences between canonically equivalent sequences.
Compatibility normalization can additionally collapse distinctions that may be meaningful for archival or linguistic evaluation.
canonical equivalence != historical equivalence != semantic equivalence.
The broader distinction between normalization and language-level transformation is treated in text normalization and transliteration .

sections.heading: 12. Character errors and word errors are nonlinear
sections.evidence: Suppose a document contains 1,000 five-character words.
paragraphs: Suppose a document contains 1,000 five-character words.
If one character error occurs in each of 50 different words, then approximately:
incorrect words = 50 total words = 1000 WER-like lexical impact ≈ 5%
If the same 50 character errors are concentrated in five badly damaged words instead, the character-level error count is unchanged while the number of corrupted words is far smaller.
CER alone does not determine word usability.

sections.heading: 13. Tokenization determines WER

paragraphs: WER is only meaningful after defining a tokenization protocol.
Is punctuation part of a word?
Are hyphenated compounds one token or multiple tokens?
How are languages without whitespace word boundaries segmented?
Are numbers tokenized as one symbol or normalized into words?
WER = OCR performance + tokenization policy + normalization policy.

paragraphs: An OCR post-corrector should not merely maximize the number of changed errors.
It must also preserve correct source text.

Character-level sequence models are attractive because they can learn variable-length OCR confusions without requiring explicit token dictionaries.

Lyu, Koutraki, Krickl, and Fetahu investigated neural post-hoc correction of historical corpora using character-level modeling and reported substantial improvement on their historical German corpus. See 10.1162/tacl_a_00379 .

sections.heading: 43. LLMs are not automatically superior post-correctors
sections.evidence: Boros, Ehrmann, Romanello, Najem-Meyer, and Kaplan evaluated fourteen foundation models on historical transcription post-correction across multiple languages and document types. Their 2024 study found that large language models were not uniformly efficient at this task despite their strength on many general text transformations. See 10.18653/v1/2024.latechclfl-1.14 .
paragraphs: Boros, Ehrmann, Romanello, Najem-Meyer, and Kaplan evaluated fourteen foundation models on historical transcription post-correction across multiple languages and document types. Their 2024 study found that large language models were not uniformly efficient at this task despite their strength on many general text transformations. See 10.18653/v1/2024.latechclfl-1.14 .
Subsequent work has continued to find strong dataset and language dependence.

Kanerva, Ledins, Käpyaho, and Ginter reported that open-weight LLMs could reduce CER on historical English data while practically useful results were harder to obtain for Finnish. See the 2025 RESOURCEFUL study .
LLM capability does not eliminate the need for OCR-specific evaluation.

sections.heading: 44. Modern LLM post-correction makes over-correction evaluation more important
sections.evidence: As post-correctors become generative, conventional CER improvement becomes insufficient.

GROUND TRUTH: In 1783 Mr. Quenouille paid £7 4s. OCR: In 1783 Mr. Quenouilie paid £7 4s.

It fixed one apparent name error but changed both identity and monetary evidence.
A fluent sentence does not reveal this damage visually.
Modern evaluation therefore needs explicit analysis of unsupported modifications in addition to aggregate error reduction.

sections.heading: 45. Current research confirms that low-noise text is especially vulnerable

paragraphs: When raw OCR is extremely noisy, a post-corrector has many opportunities to make genuine repairs.

Even a small tendency to alter correct text can then outweigh the remaining benefits.

Recent historical-document evaluation, including the 2026 HIPE-OCRepair competition, has highlighted over-correction on low-noise input as a recurring challenge. See the HIPE-OCRepair 2026 report .

sections.heading: 52. String fidelity and semantic fidelity are distinct

sections.heading: 54. Error prevalence changes the optimal threshold
sections.evidence: Consider two datasets.
paragraphs: Dataset Raw CER Correction strategy Severely degraded historical OCR 20% More aggressive correction may be beneficial High-quality modern OCR 0.3% Very conservative correction may be necessary
The same model and threshold should not automatically be deployed on both.

sections.heading: 55. Per-document adaptation can help and hurt
sections.evidence: Historical documents often contain repeated vocabulary, names, and typeface-specific errors.
paragraphs: Historical documents often contain repeated vocabulary, names, and typeface-specific errors.
Adaptation to a particular volume can exploit this structure.
may occur hundreds of times in one book.
A document-specific correction model can learn this pattern efficiently.
But evaluation must avoid learning from the same ground-truth passages that later appear in the test set.

sections.heading: 56. Correction consistency is an important secondary property
sections.evidence: If the same OCR error occurs 500 times:
paragraphs: If the same OCR error occurs 500 times:
government 420 times government. 30 times governments 20 times goverment 20 times unchanged 10 times
Context may justify some variation, but repeated systematic OCR confusions should often yield stable repairs.
Consistency analysis can therefore reveal behavior hidden by overall CER.

sections.heading: 57. Entity-sensitive evaluation
sections.evidence: Proper names are particularly vulnerable to correction models because they are rare by definition.
paragraphs: Proper names are particularly vulnerable to correction models because they are rare by definition.
A system can lower global CER while making rare entities less reliable.
For research archives, entity-specific accuracy may therefore be worth measuring separately.

sections.heading: 58. Numerical fidelity deserves separate attention
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Each may involve only one character substitution.
Yet the factual consequence can be enormous.
For invoices, scientific tables, census data, dates, legal documents, and historical records, number-specific error analysis can be more informative than generic CER alone.

sections.heading: 59. Tables require structural evaluation
sections.evidence: A table can contain every recognized character while still be unusable if cells are assigned incorrectly.
paragraphs: A table can contain every recognized character while still be unusable if cells are assigned incorrectly.
Character-level recognition may be excellent while row-column relationships are lost.
Thus OCR text evaluation and document-structure evaluation must remain distinct.

sections.heading: 60. Modern document models make this distinction even more important
sections.evidence: Contemporary OCR and document-understanding systems increasingly combine:
paragraphs: Contemporary OCR and document-understanding systems increasingly combine:
A single final text output can therefore hide errors originating in several model components.
Recent evaluation research has emphasized that historical and complex documents expose structural failures that are poorly summarized by modern-document character accuracy alone.
The 2026 survey by Beyene and Dancy reviews this evaluation problem across modern OCR and document-understanding research. See 10.1145/3805689.3806442 .

sections.heading: 61. Reproducible OCR evaluation pipeline
sections.evidence: A robust experiment should freeze the evaluation transformation.
paragraphs: A robust experiment should freeze the evaluation transformation.

REFERENCE | +--> deterministic normalization | +--> deterministic segmentation | +--> evaluation representation | +--------------------+ | v alignment ^ | +--------------------+ | OCR OUTPUT | +--> same documented normalization policy | +--> same evaluation representation
Any normalization that differs between systems compromises comparison.

sections.heading: 63. Post-correction evaluation pipeline
sections.evidence: A post-correction benchmark should preserve three distinct sequences:
paragraphs: A post-correction benchmark should preserve three distinct sequences:
G = ground truth O = original OCR C = corrected OCR
CER_before = CER(G, O) CER_after = CER(G, C)
and classify whether they were beneficial.
Did final text become closer to ground truth? and Were the changes themselves reliable?

GT: the modern Quenouille archive OCR: the modem Quenouille archive CORRECTED: the modern Grenouille archive

sections.heading: 65. Ablation experiments are essential
sections.evidence: A complex post-correction system might combine:
paragraphs: A complex post-correction system might combine:
OCR confidence + edit distance + dictionary + character error model + language model + document context
To understand what contributes to performance, compare:

Configuration Purpose Raw OCR Baseline Edit distance only Measure string-similarity contribution Edit distance + dictionary Measure lexical constraint + OCR confusion model Measure channel knowledge + language context Measure contextual contribution + confidence threshold Measure selective correction
Without ablation, aggregate improvement does not reveal which evidence source caused it.

raw CER corrected CER 0.5% 0.8% worse 3.0% 2.2% better 10.0% 5.4% much better 25.0% 12.0% much better
The correct deployment policy might therefore be:

sections.heading: 71. Re-OCR versus post-correction
sections.evidence: When source images remain available, an important alternative is to re-run OCR with a stronger recognizer.
paragraphs: When source images remain available, an important alternative is to re-run OCR with a stronger recognizer.

Situation Likely strategy Good source images + obsolete OCR Re-OCR may outperform text-only correction Images unavailable Text post-correction may be necessary Systematic lexical noise Post-correction can be effective Severe layout failure Reprocess document structure Rare historical language Conservative correction or domain adaptation Very clean OCR Correction may introduce more errors than it removes

sections.heading: 72. Ensemble OCR can provide correction evidence
sections.evidence: If multiple OCR engines transcribe the same image:
paragraphs: If multiple OCR engines transcribe the same image:
OCR A: government OCR B: govemment OCR C: government
OCR A: Quenouille OCR B: Quenouilie OCR C: Quenouille
the ensemble can protect a rare name that a generic language model might otherwise rewrite.
Ensembling is not infallible—systems can share correlated errors—but it introduces independent visual evidence unavailable to a text-only corrector.

sections.heading: 73. Confidence calibration matters
sections.evidence: Suppose a model outputs correction confidence:
paragraphs: Suppose a model outputs correction confidence:
Ideally, among corrections assigned approximately 0.95 confidence, roughly 95% should actually be valid under the evaluation definition.
If not, the confidence value is poorly calibrated.
Calibration matters because deployment thresholds depend on predicted probabilities.
A model with slightly worse CER but well-calibrated confidence may be more useful for human-assisted correction than a model whose scores cannot be trusted.

sections.heading: 74. Preserve raw OCR when automatic correction is non-reversible
sections.evidence: Never design archival processing such that:
paragraphs: Never design archival processing such that:
raw OCR -> corrected text -> raw OCR deleted.
source image | +-- raw OCR | +-- corrected OCR | +-- provenance
This allows later correction methods to be improved without losing the original machine transcription.

sections.heading: 79. The correct role of Levenshtein distance
sections.evidence: Levenshtein distance has two major roles in OCR systems.
paragraphs: Levenshtein distance has two major roles in OCR systems.
First, it provides the mathematical foundation of common sequence-error metrics:
ground truth vs. OCR output -> minimum edit alignment -> CER / WER
Second, it can support candidate generation and OCR-aware correction:
noisy token -> nearby candidate strings -> contextual / probabilistic ranking.
But these roles should not be overstated.
whether a change is semantically faithful.
It is a sequence-comparison primitive embedded inside a larger OCR evaluation or correction system.

sections.heading: 80. Final interpretation
sections.evidence: A rigorous OCR experiment should separate three questions.
paragraphs: A rigorous OCR experiment should separate three questions.

1. What text did the source contain? 2. How different is the OCR output from the chosen reference representation? 3. Can post-processing reduce genuine OCR error without changing valid source evidence?
The first question is governed by ground-truth and transcription policy.
The second can often be quantified using character- or word-level edit distance .
The third requires evaluating both improvement and damage.
OCR quality = recognition fidelity + structural fidelity + evaluation protocol + post-correction reliability + task-specific utility.

CER remains one of the most useful OCR evaluation metrics because it provides a simple, model-independent measure of sequence disagreement. But its value depends on precise definitions of character representation, normalization, ground truth, layout treatment, and aggregation.

Post-correction should likewise not be judged by fluency. A strong correction system must reduce genuine transcription error while preserving names, numbers, historical spellings, unusual vocabulary, and other evidence already recognized correctly.
post-correction should repair OCR evidence, not replace the source with what a language model believes the source probably meant.

Post-correction adds another layer of difficulty. A correction system can remove genuine OCR errors, leave errors untouched, or damage text that was already correct. A method that aggressively rewrites noisy text may reduce one aggregate edit-distance metric while destroying historically meaningful spellings, proper names, numerical values, punctuation, or document-specific terminology.
Character error rate (CER) applies edit-distance alignment at character level.
